prompt: After Schrödinger gave a seminar on de Broglie's work, what did Debye object to?

choices.text: Why a wave would confine itself to a circle, when real waves obey 3-D wave equations
That particles such as electrons could have any wave properties at all
choices.why: Debye didn't reject matter waves outright. He asked why de Broglie's waves stayed on a circle, when real waves spread out in three dimensions.

choices.text: That de Broglie's wavelength formula gave numbers that disagreed with experiment
choices.why: His complaint was not about the numbers. He asked why a wave should confine itself to a circle in space.

choices.text: That the theory used three dimensions when one dimension would be enough
choices.why: It was the reverse: Debye wanted a three-dimensional wave equation, because real waves diffract and spread out in space.

explanation: Debye called the theory childish: why should a wave confine itself to a circle in space? Real waves diffract and spread, obeying three-dimensional wave equations. Schrödinger took this as a challenge and spent some weeks building his equation.

prompt: Can the Schrödinger equation be rigorously derived from the physics known before it?

choices.text: No; it is made plausible by analogy with light waves and photons
Yes; it follows directly from Newton's laws of motion
choices.why: There is no rigorous derivation from earlier theory. The equation is made plausible by analogy, not derived from classical mechanics.

choices.text: Yes; it follows directly from the Bohr model of the atom
choices.why: The Bohr model grafts quantization onto a classical picture and cannot give the Schrödinger equation. The equation is made plausible by analogy with light and photons.

choices.text: No; it was found by fitting a formula to measured spectra
choices.why: It was not a fit to data. It was built by analogy with the link between light waves and photons.

explanation: There is no rigorous derivation of the Schrödinger equation from earlier theory. It is made plausible by building, for de Broglie's matter waves, a structure like the one that links light waves and photons, and is then postulated.

prompt: What is a weakness of the Bohr model that the Schrödinger equation overcomes?

choices.text: It is not general and grafts quantization onto classical ideas
It cannot predict the allowed energies of a hydrogen atom at all
choices.why: The Bohr model does predict the allowed energies of any one-electron atom or cation. Its weakness is that it is not general and leans on classical ideas.

choices.text: It treats the electron purely as a wave spread out through space
choices.why: Bohr's model treats the electron as a classical particle in an orbit. A better theory must include a wave-like description of particles.

choices.text: It leaves out the idea that energy is quantized altogether
choices.why: Bohr's model does quantize energy, but it clumsily adds quantization to a classical picture instead of explaining it.

explanation: The Bohr model predicts the energies of one-electron atoms, but it is not a general approach and clumsily grafts quantization onto an essentially classical picture. A better rule must account for wave-particle duality and describe particles as waves.

prompt: What is the Laplacian operator, ∇^2?

choices.why: These are first derivatives. The Laplacian adds the second derivatives with respect to x, y and z.
The three second derivatives are added, not multiplied.
The Laplacian uses only the three space coordinates. Time is not part of it.

explanation: The Laplacian, or del-squared, is the sum of the second partial derivatives with respect to x, y and z. It is the three-dimensional version of ∂^2/∂x^2.

prompt: The solution of the three-dimensional wave equation is called the wavefunction. Which variables is it a function of?

choices.text: x, y, z and t
x and t only
choices.why: That is the one-dimensional case. In three dimensions the wavefunction depends on x, y, z and t.

choices.text: x, y and z only
choices.why: A wave also changes in time, so t is a fourth variable.

choices.text: t only
choices.why: A wave varies in space as well as in time, so it depends on x, y and z too.

explanation: The solution of the 3-D wave equation is a function of four independent variables, x, y, z and t, and is generally called the wavefunction.

prompt: The wave Ψ(x) = f((2πx)/λ) repeats every time its argument increases by 2π. How far must x increase for this to happen?

choices.text: By one wavelength, λ
By 2π
choices.why: The argument grows by 2π, but x itself needs to grow only by λ, since (2π(x + λ))/λ = (2πx)/λ + 2π.

choices.text: By half a wavelength, λ/2
choices.why: Half a wavelength raises the argument by only π, half a cycle. A full cycle needs x to grow by λ.

choices.text: By λ/(2π)
choices.why: That raises the argument by only 1. To raise it by 2π, x must grow by a whole wavelength.

explanation: Sine, cosine and e^(iθ) repeat every time their argument increases by 2π. For f((2πx)/λ), this happens whenever x increases by one wavelength λ.

prompt: To turn the wave Ψ(x, t) = exp[2πi(x/λ − νt)] into a matter wave, which two relations replace ν and λ by particle properties?

choices.text: E = hν and p = h/λ
E = mc^2 and p = mv
choices.why: The section uses Planck's formula E = hν for the frequency and de Broglie's p = h/λ for the wavelength.

choices.text: E = (1/2)mv^2 and λ = v/ν
choices.why: These don't bring in Planck's constant. The replacements are Planck's E = hν and de Broglie's p = h/λ.

choices.text: c = λν and E = hc/λ
choices.why: c = λν holds for light, not for matter waves. The replacements are E = hν and p = h/λ.

explanation: Planck's formula E = hν and de Broglie's p = h/λ replace ν and λ by energy and momentum. This turns the wave into Ψ(x, t) = exp[i(px − Et)/ħ].

prompt: Why was the symbol ħ introduced?

choices.text: Planck's constant appears in most formulas divided by 2π
It is a new constant, unrelated to h, found by Schrödinger
choices.why: ħ is not new: it is h/(2π). Dirac introduced the symbol because h so often appears with 2π.

choices.text: It is a short way to write Planck's constant times 2π
choices.why: ħ is h divided by 2π, not multiplied by it.

choices.text: It is a smaller value of h that applies only to electrons
choices.why: h is the same for every particle. ħ is just h/(2π), written compactly.

explanation: ħ ≡ h/(2π). Since Planck's constant occurs in most formulas with the denominator 2π, Paul Dirac introduced the symbol ħ.

prompt: For the matter wave Ψ(x, t) = exp[i(px − Et)/ħ], which operation on Ψ gives E times Ψ?

choices.text: iħ ∂Ψ/∂t
−iħ ∂Ψ/∂x
choices.why: Differentiating with respect to x brings down p, not E: −iħ ∂Ψ/∂x = pΨ.
Two x-derivatives give p^2Ψ, the square of the momentum, not E.

choices.text: ħ × Ψ
choices.why: Multiplying by ħ just scales Ψ. The energy comes from the time derivative.

explanation: Differentiating Ψ with respect to time brings down the factor −iE/ħ, so iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = EΨ. The time derivative is linked to the energy.

prompt: For the same matter wave, Ψ(x, t) = exp[i(px − Et)/ħ], what quantity multiplies Ψ when you work out −iħ ∂Ψ/∂x?

choices.text: The momentum, p
The energy, E
choices.why: E comes from the time derivative, iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = EΨ. The x-derivative brings down p.

choices.text: The mass, m
choices.why: The mass doesn't appear in exp[i(px − Et)/ħ]. Differentiating with respect to x brings down ip/ħ.

choices.text: The momentum squared, p^2
choices.why: One x-derivative gives p. It takes a second derivative, −ħ^2 ∂^2Ψ/∂x^2 = p^2Ψ, to get p^2.

explanation: Differentiating exp[i(px − Et)/ħ] with respect to x brings down ip/ħ, so −iħ ∂Ψ/∂x = pΨ. Differentiating again gives −ħ^2 ∂^2Ψ/∂x^2 = p^2Ψ.

prompt: The equation iħ ∂Ψ/∂t = −(ħ^2/(2m)) ∂^2Ψ/∂x^2 describes what kind of particle?

choices.text: A free particle, whose potential energy does not vary
A particle held in place by a strong external force
choices.why: A force means a potential energy that varies, which would add a V(x) term. This equation has none.

choices.text: A particle moving at nearly the speed of light
choices.why: The equation was built from the nonrelativistic E = p^2/(2m), so it is for particles much slower than light.

choices.text: A photon, the particle of light, and nothing else
choices.why: It was built for de Broglie's matter waves, and it contains the particle's mass m.

explanation: It was built from E = p^2/(2m), where all the energy is kinetic. So it describes a free particle: one not bound by external forces, in a region where its potential energy does not vary.

prompt: In the time-independent Schrödinger equation, [−(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2 + V(r⃗)]ψ(r⃗) = Eψ(r⃗), which term stands for the kinetic energy?

choices.text: V(r⃗)
choices.why: V(r⃗) is the potential energy, which depends on position. The kinetic energy comes from the second-derivative term.

choices.text: E
choices.why: E is the total energy, kinetic plus potential.

choices.text: −(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2 + V(r⃗), the whole bracket
choices.why: The whole bracket is kinetic plus potential energy, which gives the total. Only the ∇^2 term is the kinetic energy.

explanation: The −(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2 term comes from p^2/(2m), the kinetic energy. V(r⃗) is the potential energy, and E is the total energy.

prompt: In the three-dimensional Schrödinger equation, what does r⃗ stand for?

choices.text: The three space coordinates x, y and z
The radius of the electron's circular orbit
choices.why: r⃗ is not an orbit radius. It is shorthand for the position (x, y, z).

choices.text: The time t at which Ψ is evaluated
choices.why: Time is written separately, as in Ψ(r⃗, t). r⃗ stands for x, y and z.

choices.text: Only the distance from the nucleus
choices.why: r⃗ is the full position, all three coordinates x, y and z, not just a distance.

explanation: The potential energy and the wavefunction depend on the three space coordinates x, y and z, which are written for brevity as r⃗.

prompt: In the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, what is the potential energy V(r⃗) assumed to depend on?

choices.text: Position only, not time
Time only, not position
choices.why: It's the other way round: V(r⃗) depends on position only. This holds for conservative forces.

choices.text: The particle's momentum
choices.why: V is written V(r⃗), a function of position alone.

choices.text: Both position and time
choices.why: V is assumed not to change with time, which holds for conservative forces.

explanation: The potential energy is assumed to depend on position only, not on time. This applies to conservative forces, for which a potential energy function V(r⃗) can be written.

prompt: When the del operator ∇ acts directly on a field, as in ∇f(x, y, z), what does it give?

choices.text: The gradient: the locally steepest slope
The area under the field, found by integrating
choices.why: ∇ is built from first derivatives, not integrals. It gives the gradient, the steepest slope.

choices.text: The Laplacian of the field, ∇^2f
choices.why: The Laplacian is ∇^2 = ∇·∇, which takes ∇ twice. ∇ alone gives the gradient.

choices.text: The average value of the field over all space
choices.why: ∇ is made of first derivatives, so it measures a slope, not an average.

explanation: ∇ = x⃗ ∂/∂x + y⃗ ∂/∂y + z⃗ ∂/∂z, where x⃗, y⃗ and z⃗ are unit vectors. Acting on a field, it gives the gradient, the locally steepest slope. Applied twice, ∇·∇, it gives the Laplacian ∇^2.

prompt: The Schrödinger equation of 1926 marks the start of modern quantum mechanics. What other version had Heisenberg proposed in 1925?

choices.text: Matrix mechanics
Quantum electrodynamics
choices.why: Quantum electrodynamics came later: it combines the Schrödinger equation with a quantum description of the electromagnetic field.

choices.text: The Bohr model
choices.why: Bohr's model (1913) is the older picture that Schrödinger's approach replaced. Heisenberg's 1925 version was matrix mechanics.

choices.text: The classical wave equation
choices.why: The wave equation for light comes from Maxwell's classical electromagnetism, not from Heisenberg.

explanation: Schrödinger formulated his equation in 1926, the start of modern quantum mechanics. Heisenberg had proposed another version in 1925, known as matrix mechanics.

prompt: When can the time-dependent factor of Ψ(r⃗, t) be separated from its space-only factor?

choices.text: When the system is conservative (constant energy)
Only when the particle is completely at rest
choices.why: Moving particles can have separable wavefunctions too. What matters is that the energy is constant.

choices.text: Only when the potential energy is zero at every point
choices.why: V(r⃗) can be nonzero; it just must not change with time, so that the energy is constant.

choices.text: Never; the time and space parts always stay mixed together
choices.why: For conservative systems they do separate: Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗)e^(−iEt/ħ).

explanation: For a conservative system the energy is constant, and separation of variables splits the wavefunction into a space part times a time part: Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗)e^(−iEt/ħ).

prompt: For a conservative system, Ψ(r⃗, t) is ψ(r⃗) times a time factor. What is the time factor?

choices.text: e^(−iEt/ħ)
e^(−Et/ħ)
choices.why: The exponent includes i. Without it the factor would decay away in time instead of oscillating.

choices.text: e^(ipx/ħ)
choices.why: That depends on x, not t. The time factor is e^(−iEt/ħ).

choices.text: Et/ħ
choices.why: The time dependence is a complex exponential, e^(−iEt/ħ), not a simple product.

explanation: Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗)e^(−iEt/ħ). Putting this into the time-dependent equation and canceling the exponential factors leaves the time-independent Schrödinger equation.

prompt: In terms of energy, what does the time-independent Schrödinger equation say?

choices.text: Kinetic plus potential energy equals the total energy
Kinetic energy is always equal to potential energy
choices.why: The two are added, not set equal: kinetic plus potential gives the total energy E.

choices.text: The total energy changes steadily as time passes
choices.why: In the time-independent equation the energy E is a constant.

choices.text: The total energy of every system must be zero
choices.why: E is the total energy and can take various values. The equation says that kinetic plus potential energy equals E.

explanation: The time-independent Schrödinger equation is built on the conservation of energy: the system's kinetic energy plus its potential energy equals its total energy, just as in classical physics.

prompt: Which equation are most applications of quantum mechanics to chemistry based on?

choices.text: The time-independent Schrödinger equation
The time-dependent equation, even for stable molecules
choices.why: Most applications in chemistry use the time-independent equation. The main exception is spectroscopy.

choices.text: The free-particle equation, with V set to zero
choices.why: The electrons in atoms and molecules have potential energy, so the full time-independent equation, with V(r⃗), is used.

choices.text: The classical wave equation for light
choices.why: That equation describes electromagnetic waves, not the matter waves of electrons.

explanation: Most applications of quantum mechanics to chemistry are based on the time-independent Schrödinger equation, [−(ħ^2/(2m))∇^2 + V(r⃗)]ψ(r⃗) = Eψ(r⃗). The exception is spectroscopy.

prompt: A wavefunction ψ(r⃗) from the time-independent equation has no t in it. Does that mean it has no time dependence at all?

choices.text: No; the full Ψ(r⃗, t) has a phase factor that varies in time
Yes; a state described by ψ(r⃗) is completely frozen in time
choices.why: Every wavefunction has a time dependence. Here it sits in the phase factor e^(−iEt/ħ).

choices.text: Yes; only light waves, not matter waves, can depend on time
choices.why: Matter waves depend on time too, through the factor e^(−iEt/ħ).

choices.text: No; ψ(r⃗) itself grows steadily larger as time passes
choices.why: The time factor has a constant magnitude: it oscillates, it doesn't grow.

explanation: The full wavefunction is Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗)e^(−iEt/ħ). It differs from ψ(r⃗) by a phase factor of constant magnitude, which in simple problems often doesn't affect the results and can be ignored.

prompt: The full wavefunction Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗)(cos(Et/ħ) − i sin(Et/ħ)) has a real part and an imaginary part. How do they behave in time?

choices.text: Both oscillate, with the imaginary part out of phase by π/2
Only the real part oscillates; the imaginary part is fixed
choices.why: Both oscillate: one goes as cos(Et/ħ), the other as sin(Et/ħ).

choices.text: Both oscillate exactly in step with each other
choices.why: They are shifted by π/2, since sin θ = cos(θ − π/2).

choices.text: Neither part changes as time passes
choices.why: cos(Et/ħ) and sin(Et/ħ) both change as t increases.

explanation: Using sin θ = cos(θ − π/2), Ψ(r⃗, t) = ψ(r⃗) cos(Et/ħ) − iψ(r⃗) cos(Et/ħ − π/2). Both parts oscillate, and the imaginary part is out of phase by π/2 with the real part.

prompt: How well has quantum theory held up under experimental tests?

choices.text: It agrees with every case studied to better than 10^−10 %
It works for hydrogen but fails for larger atoms
choices.why: No failures are known: in every case studied it agrees with experiment to better than 10^−10 %.

choices.text: It has never been tested, because it is too abstract
choices.why: Despite its weirdness, quantum theory has been subject to intense experimental scrutiny.

choices.text: It agrees with experiment only to within about 10%
choices.why: The agreement is far better than that: better than 10^−10 %.

explanation: Quantum theory has been found to agree with experiments to better than 10^−10 % in every case studied so far. Combined with a quantum description of the electromagnetic field, as quantum electrodynamics, it is one of the most accurate theories of matter ever put forth.

prompt: ħ is defined as h/(2π). With h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s, what is ħ, in J·s? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
For a free particle, all the energy is kinetic: E = p^2/(2m). A particle has m = 9.0 × 10^−31 kg and p = 3.0 × 10^−24 kg·m/s. What is its energy, in J? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
For a free particle, E = p^2/(2m). If the particle's momentum doubles, by what factor does its energy increase?
explanation: E is proportional to p^2, so doubling p multiplies E by 2^2 = 4.

prompt: For a particle with potential energy, E = p^2/(2m) + V(x). A particle has total energy E = 5.0 eV at a point where V = 1.5 eV. What is its kinetic energy, p^2/(2m), there, in eV?
explanation: The total energy is kinetic plus potential, so p^2/(2m) = E − V = 5.0 eV − 1.5 eV = 3.5 eV.

prompt: To build a matter wave, the section replaces λ by momentum using de Broglie's p = h/λ. With h = 6.626 × 10^−34 J·s, what is p for λ = 1.0 × 10^−10 m, in kg·m/s? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-19.)
The function f(x, y, z) = sin(3x) depends only on x, so ∂^2f/∂y^2 and ∂^2f/∂z^2 are both zero. Applying the Laplacian gives ∇^2f = (a number) × f. What is the number?
explanation: ∂f/∂x = 3cos(3x), and ∂^2f/∂x^2 = −9sin(3x). The y and z terms are zero, so ∇^2f = −9f.

prompt: Euler's formula says e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. Using cos π = −1 and sin π = 0, what is e^(iπ)?
explanation: e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1 + i × 0 = −1. The imaginary part vanishes, leaving a real number.
